## Context and commentary

Laurent Lafforgue (a Canadian mathematician working in France and the grand prize winner for the 2017 French mathematical competition EFTEM) made predictions in 2007 related to this question, covering six different mathematical topics. He stated at least 50% conversion of progress whether or not any prize was eventually awarded, and gave the following probabilities at the given deadlines. This forecasts events accruing into ranges of dates including years, even as has been informally suggested elsewhere, so perhaps long-answer forecasts in addition to probabilities could be interesting and popular.

- 2020: 25% Solved NP=P, 25% Other solutions will be possibly correct but disputed, 25% will solve Yet Another Hard Mathematical Problem
- 2025: 50% Still 50-50 on NP=P
- 2030: 75% if legacy prevents progress, borrow from AI
- 2035: 50-50 split acceptably acceptable without external evidence, so long answer posts?
- 2040: put all of history on a silver platter
- 2045: you will have all the answers within reach
- 2050: critical corner cases in quantum computers

Interestingly, discussion of Lafforgue's work focusing on his earlier predictions and their apparent correlation with later events often misunderstands several topical subjects. The probability distributions he gave for 2025 and 2030 are identical. He explicitly stated that NP=P was the same question for him at both dates. Citers who want his opinion engaged in debates on CA are advised to understand why exactly this forecasting strategy seems to have been chosen. Even with all this in mind, Lafforgue gave explicit low probabilities for NA and NP, well below the base rates.

It is interesting that Lafforges' probability for 2026 was just a little bit higher than mine, but his 2030 probability is just a little lower than mine. This, and his more thorough numerical modeling, might be regarded as an indication that Lafforge's judgment and insight are better than mine (should anyone be interested).

It is also interesting that Lafforge did not plan on the millennium prize problems being solved, at very least in his lifetime. <|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2025-04-29. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

For each deadline, state your probability that this event will have occurred by then. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
